newsitem.title: GERMANY: U.S. soldier on rape charges in Germany.
newsitem.headline: U.S. soldier on rape charges in Germany.

text.p: A U.S. military prosecutor on Monday accused an army sergeant of using his rank to rape, sodomise and harrass women soldiers at a base in Germany and also during his unit's service in Bosnia.

Army prosecutor Major Michael Klausner told a court martial of Sergeant Julius Davis that police found Davis had a long history of sexual abuse after a female soldier made a complaint about him last November.
Klausner said another female soldier would testify that Davis, her superior, made lewd comments to her while on duty in Bosnia and also made her visit his tent and had tried, but failed, to rape her.

Davis, who pleaded not guilty, is one of three sergeants accused of sex-related crimes at the Darmstadt base, where soldiers spend two weeks on an orientation course after arriving in Germany. The male commander of the centre has been replaced by a woman.

The trial is the latest sex scandal to hit the U.S. military, and the first outside the United States, since last November when allegations of harassment and rape first surfaced at the Aberdeen Proving Ground military base in Maryland.
Three staff members at the military post convicted this year of having sex with female trainees included one sergeant who was sentenced to 25 years in prison.

Another recent sex case, which pitted the Air Force against its first woman bomber pilot, Lieutenant Kelly Flinn, has prompted an emotional debate over the military's strict rules on relationships between men and women.

Defence attorneys did not mention race as a possible motivation for the charges against Davis, as had been made in the Aberdeen cases. But they selected the panel of jurors on the basis of their views on interracial dating.
Davis, 37, from Fayetteville, North Carolina, is black. Most of the women who have made allegations against Davis were white and of lower military rank, according to army officials.

A defence attorney charged army prosecutors with creating a "paper tiger" case against Davis and that female soldiers who had consensual sexual relations with him were coerced into saying they were raped.
"What the government has done is gone out and searched for witnesses and seek to build a case that does not exist," Army Major Linda Taylor told the all-male five-member military jury.

"This was a witch-hunt by investigators. If you can find consent on the part of the women, you cannot convict," Taylor said. "He is a single man who women found very attractive and wanted to be with him."
Taylor said prosecutors had no medical evidence to prove accusations of rape. In later testimony, a military police investigator conceded there was no medical evidence to back up the accusations.

Taylor also said nine investigators spent more than 4,000 manhours of taxpayer's money on the case and that only one of at least a dozen women who will testify had voluntarily come forward to make allegations against Davis.

But Klausner said several witnesses would testify that Davis had forced them to have sex with him or touched them in an intimate manner starting from his time as a drill instructor in the United States at a base in Indiana in the early 1990s.
